The Art of Making an Entrance

Some cars are designed to be driven. Others are designed to be admired. The TVR Tuscan was designed to make absolutely certain you never forgot seeing it. And unlike so many automotive showmen, it had the performance to justify every bit of the spectacle.

By Grayson Kollen · 17 minute read

360 bhp
From TVR’s own 4.0-liter straight-six
3.9 sec
0–60 mph, TVR’s claim for the 4.0
850+
Orders at its 1998 debut, nearly twice the Griffith’s
160
Mk2s built. The encore nobody stayed for

There are automobiles that attract attention, and then there are automobiles that seem incapable of existing without it. The TVR Tuscan belongs firmly in the second category. Imagine walking through a parking lot full of Porsches, Mercedes-Benzes and BMWs, perhaps a Ferrari, and suddenly stopping, not because you recognize the badge but because you can’t quite work out what you’re looking at.

The paint seems to change color as you approach. The nose is impossibly smooth, interrupted by round openings and headlights placed wherever the designer fancied, and the body looks sculpted rather than drawn. At the back, 2 big exhaust pipes emerge like the barrels of a pair of shotguns, and inside, the dashboard could have come from a futuristic aircraft. Then you notice the badge. Not Maranello, not Stuttgart, not Sant’Agata Bolognese, but Blackpool, England, and somehow that makes the whole thing even more extraordinary.

This is the Tuscan, a car that embodied nearly everything wonderful, outrageous, ambitious and occasionally infuriating about TVR. It was fast enough to challenge the supercars of its day, and it could test the patience, bank account and mechanical sympathy of even its most devoted owner. Whether you loved it or hated it, there was virtually no chance you would ignore it.

The briefTVR’s great leap forward

To understand why it mattered, remember where TVR stood in the 1990s. The Griffith and Chimaera had made Peter Wheeler’s company famous for light, ferociously powerful sports cars at modest prices, and the Cerbera had shown it could be far more ambitious. But the roadsters had become weekend cars, wonderful on a sunny Sunday and demanding in the wet, and Wheeler wanted a new generation of TVRs that people could use every day. The Tuscan was meant to lead it. That is one of the great ironies of the car: it was supposed to represent a more mature TVR, and it ended up looking like something from another planet. Thank goodness it did.

Act 1The Griffith that wasn’t

It didn’t start life as the Tuscan. At the 1997 London Motor Show, TVR displayed a yellow Griffith Speed Six, the familiar roadster updated with new front and rear ends, a new interior and a tail with more than a hint of Porsche Boxster about it. The real news was under the hood: TVR’s new 4.0-liter Speed Six, an all-aluminum, 24-valve straight-six with dry-sump lubrication, a racing feature almost unheard of on a road car, designed by Al Melling with John Ravenscroft and Wheeler himself. Around 400 people ordered one.

None of them got one. Wheeler, according to Ralph Dodds in TVR: Cars of the Peter Wheeler Era, didn’t like the way it looked, and after designer Damian McTaggart had reworked it, the revised Griffith was abandoned, just as the V8 Griffith AJP had been a few years earlier. Instead, TVR built a new car on a shortened Cerbera chassis with the bigger car’s suspension and brakes. It kept TVR’s recipe of a steel-tube frame, fiberglass body, front engine, manual gearbox and rear-wheel drive, but almost everything else was new, and Wheeler’s brief was clear. As he explained at the 1999 London Motor Show, it had to work as an everyday car, comfortable enough for 2 people to tour for 2 weeks.

The costumeA designer’s imagination without adult supervision

The Tuscan is not a conventionally beautiful car, and I mean that as a compliment. McTaggart’s starting point was refreshingly honest: “I started with a Griff and just reworked it with Photoshop.” Wheeler preferred to judge every idea at full size, and McTaggart’s notes from the time, scrawled across photographs of a Griffith, ask for better engine cooling in slow traffic and, in one corner, mourn the old 1970s-style badge. Where the Cerbera has a long, elegant profile, the Tuscan’s nose rolls downward in almost organic curves, the front fenders rise around the headlights and the tail looks as though it was shaped by the wind. There are very few hard edges, yet it never looks soft. It looks alive.

The Mk1’s face is unforgettable. Instead of a conventional grille, TVR cut a pattern of round holes across the nose that enthusiasts called the cheese grater, some affectionately and some less so, with round lights stacked on either side of the hood. Out back, 2 huge superbike-style exhausts, Wheeler’s own idea, popped and banged on the overrun. Richard Meaden of evo summed it up: “The styling is utterly outrageous, even by TVR’s outlandish standards.” To some it was bizarre. To others, me included, it was magnificent.

The Tuscan wasn’t trying to be a prettier Porsche 911, a cheaper Ferrari 360 or a British take on the Honda NSX. It was trying to be a Tuscan, and TVR seemed to ask what would happen if it simply ignored everyone’s expectations. That is also why it has aged so well. Its body was dramatic because of its shape, not because anyone decorated it with wings and vents, and a car that never followed the trends of its era is very hard to date. Unveil a carefully updated Tuscan at a motor show today, and I suspect people would still ask whether it was brand new.

The paintThe color of trouble

The bodywork was only half the performance. The paint did the rest. The Tuscan’s pearlescent and color-shifting finishes changed with the light and the angle, purple to blue, blue to green, bronze to gold, so a Tuscan parked in the sun could look like several different cars as you walked around it. In a world of silver German sedans, it was an explosion of color, and even in plain blue, black, white or yellow, it was always unmistakably a Tuscan.

The paint was part of the act from the very first night. When the Tuscan made its public debut at the Birmingham Motor Show in October 1998, it wore TVR’s chameleon finish, and more than 850 customers ordered one at £38,000 ($63,000), about £86,800 ($115,100) in 2026 money. That was nearly twice as many orders as the Griffith had drawn at its own debut 8 years earlier, and most of the Griffith Speed Six orders carried across, too.

Backstage at Bristol Avenue

The week before. Work on a TVR show car only started in earnest about a week before opening, production engineer Trevor Cooper remembered, because Wheeler, smoking one cigarette after another, could never settle on what he wanted. The team practically moved into the factory, and trimmer Chris McGuire remembered Wheeler turning up at all hours of the night with pizza for everyone.

The vacation. One year, Cooper took his vacation in the run-up to a show. Wheeler’s reaction made sure he never did it again.

The 15-degree line. Type-approval rules demanded a clear 15-degree line from the bottom of each rear indicator to the road, so TVR got the original Tuscan certified with a trunk lid that had a 30 mm (1.2 in) cut in it. Former staff admit they used to “cheat all the time,” and Ravenscroft reckoned no TVR exhaust would ever have passed the noise rules, which was exactly why people loved them.

The roofA grand tourer dressed as a spaceship

For all its theater, the Tuscan was meant to be a usable road car, and the roof shows it. Since the 1980 Tasmin convertible, TVR’s open cars had used a folding rear hoop and screen with a separate targa panel. The Tuscan kept a removable roof panel but made the rear hoop a fixed structure with a lift-out glass rear window, so you could have a snug semi-fixed roof, open air with the hoop still behind you, or something very close to a roadster, with both pieces stowed in the trunk. It was nothing like pressing a button on a modern folding hardtop, but it was a distinctly TVR solution.

It was safer, too. After a small number of serious rollover accidents in Griffiths and Chimaeras, the Tuscan, like the Cerbera, built rollover protection into the windshield frame and the rear structure. There was still no ABS and no airbag, because Wheeler believed such aids made drivers lazy, but this was a sports car trying to combine exotic performance with genuine touring practicality. It was a showman, but a showman who could pack a suitcase.

The cabinAn interior from a future that never happened

Open the door and the spectacle continues. The cockpit bears almost no resemblance to the businesslike interiors Porsche, BMW and Mercedes-Benz were building at the time, and once again I mean that as a compliment. The dashboard is a sweep of curved surfaces, exposed metal and round instruments, and where the Griffith and Chimaera had worn wood, the Tuscan mixed leather with stainless steel, brushed aluminum and brass. Even the hood played along: open it and you found only a service hatch, because reaching the engine meant unbolting the whole thing. The controls could confuse and build quality varied, but the cabin stayed remarkably faithful to the prototype, and in an industry where so many cars share their switches, it is hard to criticize TVR for trying. Character is increasingly difficult to manufacture.

The voiceThe engine that made the Tuscan, and nearly broke TVR

Beneath all that was an engine almost as ambitious as the design. The Speed Six was a 4.0-liter, all-aluminum straight-six with twin overhead camshafts, 4 valves per cylinder and a dry sump, built by TVR itself at Bristol Avenue. Most performance makers favored V8s or turbochargers, but Wheeler believed a British sports car should have a straight-six, as the great Jaguars, Aston Martins and Austin-Healeys had, and a straight-six is naturally well balanced. Its drawback is length, but the Tuscan’s long hood let TVR lean the engine over about 30 degrees, which freed up footwell space and let the catalytic converters sit close enough to the engine to warm up quickly for the emissions tests. Writing in Autocar in July 2003, David Vivian still rated it “one of the world’s best half-dozen performance engines.”

BackstageWhen 300 horsepower wasn’t enough

The original plan called for about 300 bhp, and the first engine delivered it. Then Wheeler drove an early development car and came back with a 4-word verdict: “It needs more power.” The production 4.0 ended up with a claimed 360 bhp at 7,000 rpm and 310 lb-ft of torque at 5,250, exceptional for a naturally aspirated engine of its size, but wringing that much from an all-new design created problems TVR struggled to solve.

The worst involved the finger followers, the small swinging arms that pass each cam lobe’s push to its valve. They are lighter than the usual bucket type, but they always wear in the same spot, so they are prone to scuffing. Chief engineer John Ravenscroft explained that the first versions had a hard carbide pad that worked loose after about 10,000 miles, and their heat-treated iron replacements sometimes scuffed with no obvious pattern. It took another change of materials to cure it, while suppliers closed and their replacements built parts to slightly different specifications. TVR even considered scrapping the engine, until Wheeler argued that with so many already on the road, repairing them made more sense.

The cost was brutal. McTaggart reckoned a couple of warranty claims wiped out the profit on a car, and some cars came back 3 or 4 times. At one stage, more than 20 engineless Tuscans sat outside a factory shed, and a rebuild could take up to 3 months. Not every engine failed; in 2014, Dodds was shown an early car at X-Works Service near Preston with 95,000 miles and no major engine work. By the later years most of the problems had been solved, but reputations are harder to rebuild than engines.

It didn’t help that the dry-sump Speed Six was closer to a racing engine than a road car’s. You couldn’t start one from cold and head for the redline, and even long idling did the followers no favors, so TVR’s former service manager Paul Forrest advised driving away gently at about 2,000 rpm until the oil was warm. None of that excuses the defects. When the engine worked, it was magnificent. When it didn’t, the engine that made the Tuscan so fast also helped undermine the company that built it.

The stuntsPerformance that embarrassed the establishment

The styling grabbed the headlines, but the performance earned them. TVR claimed 0–60 mph in about 3.9 seconds for the 4.0 and a top speed of 195 mph. At the turn of the millennium, Ferrari’s 360 Modena had 400 PS (395 hp), Porsche’s original 996 GT3 had 360 PS (355 hp), and Aston Martin’s DB7 Vantage had a 420 PS V12 and far more weight to carry. The Tuscan belonged in that company, and it cost about £38,000 at launch, when the Ferrari and the Porsche would each soon cost around £70,000.

It could handle, too. Chief chassis engineer Neill Anderson set out to tame the oversteer that had made earlier TVRs so unforgiving, and he did it so well that he could later say, “It’s actually quite difficult to drive a Cerbera or Tuscan sideways.” Paul Horrell of Car, who had once doubted TVRs were for him at all, drove one through the Pennines and Cumbria in miserable weather and put it “in the 360 Modena or 911 GT3 league.” Meaden drove the same press car, W998 AFR, and went further: in his view, the GT3 was the one that should be nervous.

Wheeler and Anderson even worried they had made it too tame, but tame is relative. With no traction control, no stability control and no ABS, just a 5-speed manual sending everything to the rear wheels, it was far friendlier than a Griffith and still demanded respect, especially in the wet. It offered supercar performance without the insulation the supercar world was starting to wrap around its drivers, and that was both its glory and its danger.

The encoreThe Red Rose and the Tuscan S: because apparently 360 horsepower wasn’t enough

You would think a car that could reach 60 mph in about 4 seconds might be enough. Not for TVR. The Red Rose version, a badge borrowed from the Cerbera, added about 20 bhp, bigger brakes and upgraded suspension, and between 10 and 15 percent of Tuscans are thought to have been built that way. Then, in April 2001, came the Tuscan S, with 390 bhp, later 400, 60 mph in under 4 seconds and a claimed top speed just short of 200 mph (320 km/h), from a targa-topped sports car built in Blackpool.

Angus Frazer, testing it for Top Gear, reckoned only a track would let you find the end of it, rated it alongside the Pagani Zonda C12S and the Lamborghini Diablo 6.0 VT, and joked that his long-term Subaru WRX felt like a Ford Transit van afterward. At £48,880 ($70,400), about £104,900 ($139,200) in 2026 money, the S cost 22 percent more than a standard Tuscan, by then a 3.6. But a 911 GT3 or a 360 Modena cost around £70,000 ($100,800) before options, and on TVR’s figures the S carried far more power for every kilogram than either.

Its rear spoiler carried a Gurney flap that proved its worth in the wind tunnel, pressing the tail down for real. That is the wonderful contrast at the heart of the car. For all the drama, its engineers knew a car approaching 200 mph needed stability, brakes and a chassis to match, and the fact that it looked like something from the future was almost incidental. Almost.

Act 2The Mk2: when the showman learned some manners

By 2004, TVR had learned a great deal from the original. The Mk2 arrived at that year’s NEC Motor Show alongside a new full convertible, both with the 350 bhp 3.6 and both priced at £39,850 ($73,000), about £79,400 ($105,300) in 2026 money, barely 5 percent more than the original Tuscan in 1998. The cheese grater gave way to a more conventional opening, the headlights were regrouped into new pods, the interior was updated, and the Mk2 gained an electric power-steering pump from the Tamora and T350 along with revised suspension geometry. The convertible, which many saw as the true heir to the Griffith, brought back TVR’s classic 2-piece roof with a rollover hoop behind each seat.

The 400 bhp Mk2 S added a Le Mans-inspired splitter, a bigger Gurney flap, 18-inch wheels and air conditioning for £49,995 ($91,600), about £99,600 ($132,100) today, and it was the first production car in Britain with a digital radio as standard. evo found the revised Tuscan flatter under braking and acceleration and far calmer on wet roads, and Chris Thorp of Auto Express called the TVR “hard to match for thrills per pound.” In many ways, it was the car Wheeler had wanted all along.

Was it better-looking? On the Mk1, the strange details are its identity, and the Mk2 cleaned them up. The convertible in particular is handsome, and I understand why buyers preferred it. But something was lost, and it wasn’t beauty. It was character. The Mk1 looked as if it had no interest in being accepted by the establishment, and the Mk2 looked as if someone had finally persuaded it to behave. To drive every day, I’d take a carefully maintained late Mk2. To capture everything that made TVR so gloriously individual, it would have to be a Mk1, ideally in a color-shifting paint.

The what-ifThe Tuscan that might have saved TVR

The later cars raise one of the most frustrating questions in TVR’s history: what if they had come sooner? By 2004 the engine had been sorted and the chassis refined, but the momentum of that first night in Birmingham was long gone. Reliability worries, warranty costs and fading confidence had sent buyers elsewhere, and only about 160 Mk2s were built, half targas and half convertibles, against at least 10 times as many Mk1s.

Dodds goes as far as calling the Mk2, in convertible form above all, a contender for the best car TVR ever made. Production ran until the Blackpool factory closed in December 2006, with a few late Mk3s wearing the T350’s curving dashboard and a handful of cars finished by dealers after the doors had shut.

The characterThe showman

Every great TVR has its own place in the family portrait. There is the Griffith, the hot rod, and the Chimaera, the spy on holiday. The Cerbera is the family man with a criminal record, the Tamora the weekend escape artist and the Sagaris the assassin. The Tuscan is the showman, the star who walks onstage in something outrageous, captures everyone’s attention and then delivers a performance that justifies the spectacle. Its engine was extraordinary, even if its reliability was not, and its performance was astonishing next to far costlier machinery. It was outrageous in almost every respect, but it wasn’t pretending. There is a difference between a car that looks fast and a car that is fast, and the Tuscan managed to be both.

Curtain callThe final act

Imagine arriving at a gathering of Ferraris, Porsches, Aston Martins and Lamborghinis, every badge with a reputation. Then a Tuscan pulls in, its paint catching the afternoon sun and its straight-six rasping as it eases into a space. People drift over. Someone asks about the engine, someone else where it was built, and a third can’t understand how a car like this could possibly have come from Blackpool. The owner smiles, because the questions are familiar, and because it is deeply satisfying to drive something that can still surprise people more than a quarter of a century later.

The Tuscan was never the sensible choice. It never offered the predictability of a Porsche, the prestige of a Ferrari or the refinement of an Aston Martin. What it offered was an almost complete refusal to conform, which made it spectacular, made it difficult and shaped both the rise and the troubles of the company that built it. It deserves to be remembered as the moment British automotive imagination ran almost unchecked, when a small company took on the world’s great performance brands with a car that looked like a concept, went like a supercar and could still take 2 people away for 2 weeks.

The Griffith made TVR exciting. The Cerbera made TVR ambitious. But the Tuscan made TVR impossible to ignore. It didn’t merely enter the room. It changed the atmosphere, and long after the lights went down, the audience was still talking about it.

If you want one

You can bring one home now. The earliest customer cars, from 2000 onward, are now turning 25, old enough to import into the US under the 25-year rule. One 2000 car imported in January 2026 sold on Bring a Trailer that May for about £33,400 by The Classic Valuer’s conversion, roughly $44,000. Our guide The Long Road Home explains how.

What they cost in Britain. Over the past year, a 28,000-mile, one-owner 2000 car sold for £20,812 ($27,600), a pampered 25,000-mile car fetched £35,500 ($47,100), and a project with a running fault went for £11,788 ($15,600).

Warm it, then drive it. Ask what was done to the finger followers and when, check the chassis for rust, budget as you would for a 1960s exotic, and drive away gently at about 2,000 rpm until the oil is warm.

Some automobiles are remembered for their performance. Others for their beauty. The truly extraordinary ones give us a story worth telling.
